newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Year's third general strike staged in Argentina.
newsitem.headline: Year's third general strike staged in Argentina.

text.p: Argentine unions unleashed their third general strike in four months on Thursday in a nation still groggy after Christmas celebrations, but the government said it was minor and would change nothing.

White-collar workers sweated in traffic jams under a blazing summer sun as many were forced to take cars to work by disrupted bus and train services. But shoppers crowded central Buenos Aires and banks and offices worked as usual.
As the day drew to a close, local media reported varying levels of support for the strike in the provinces.
Union leaders, who launched the strike to protest decrees to make labour markets more flexible, crowed that they had brought industry to a halt, but the government was dismissive.

"The turnout was at least 83 percent and we thank and salute the working people and the immense majority of the Argentine people," the head of the CGT labour federation Rodolfo Daer told reporters late afternoon.
But the Labour Ministry said only about 31 percent of Argentine workers had joined the stoppage.
President Carlos Menem had vowed to ignore the strike, which he described as a meaningless move cynically scheduled for the day after Christmas, when many do not work anyway.

The CGT, which long had a cosy relationship with Menem's Peronist Party and has been criticised by more left-wing groups for shying away from confrontation, called no demonstration to accompany the strike.

The government said 42 percent of urban public transport was halted, down from 61 percent in a strike on Sept. 27. Flights at Buenos Aires' domestic airport were almost halved as pilots stayed away but international flights merely suffered delays.

Some buses had windows smashed by angry unionists but no serious incidents were reported. The CGT called its third strike this year after Menem lost patience with talks with the unions to hammer out a compromise over the laws, which would reduce employers' costs.

The president passed the laws by decree, provoking unions into following up a 24-hour stoppage in August against Menem's free-market policies and their successful September strike. The government, which said it plans more labour decrees, hopes a more flexible employment market will help reduce the country's 17.3 percent jobless rate.

The laws allow workers to decide which union health plan they sign up for and permit smaller firms to bypass national unions in wage talks with workers. Employers can apply to the government if they want to negotiate with unions on a company-by-company instead of an industrywide basis.
